extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers, magazine editors, and literary readers interested in criteria for selecting/assessing short fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and procedural rules for selecting, grouping, and republishing American short stories for an annual anthology (period covered: Oct 1919–Sep 1920). Emphasis on literary quality (substance and form), sincerity, and avoidance of formulaic or commercial fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first test of a short story... is to report upon how vitally compelling the writer makes his selected facts or incidents. This test may be conveniently called the test of substance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance means 'organic substance'—material in which 'the pulse of life is beating.' Facts only attain substantial embodiment when the artist's power of 'compelling imaginative persuasion' transforms them into a living truth. Evaluate whether the writer's selected facts/incidents are made vitally compelling to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of form
rubrics_metrics.description: "A second test is necessary... The true artist will seek to shape this living substance into the most beautiful and satisfying form, by skilful selection and arrangement of his materials, and by the most direct and appealing presentation of it in portrayal and characterization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the story shapes its substance: skillful selection and arrangement of material, direct and appealing presentation, effective portrayal and characterization, and overall aesthetic/formal unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic substance (not inorganic fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No substance is of importance in fiction, unless it is organic substance, that is to say, substance in which the pulse of life is beating. Inorganic fiction has been our curse..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stories whose subject-matter is organically integrated with form and dramatic life; avoid superficially plotted or merely contrived (inorganic) fiction that lacks a living core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and imaginative reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in 'the fresh, living current which flows through the best of our work, and the psychological and imaginative reality which our writers have conferred upon it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value stories that convey convincing inner life, believable psychology, and an imaginative reality that makes characters and situations feel alive and authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / authorial earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek 'the man and woman with something to say... who cares very much indeed about how he says it... I want to feel that the storyteller... is as much in earnest as a sincere clergyman... I want to feel that he belongs to a profession that is a sort of priesthood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authors who 'mean what they say' and write with genuine conviction and seriousness rather than commercial calculation or affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of formula and commercialism
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am not at all interested in formulae, and organised criticism at its best would be nothing more than dead criticism..."; criticism of 'the excessive commercialisation of literature' and 'magazines which bought and sold fiction like soap.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject formulaic, mass-produced, or overtly commercial fiction. Favor work that resists hackneyed formulae and displays artistic discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sloppy sentimentality and slapstick farce
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sloppy sentimentality and slapstick farce ought to bore us frightfully... Life is too real to go to sleep over it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devalue stories relying on cheap sentiment, mawkishness, or crude farce; favor seriousness and truthful engagement with life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive viewpoint & attention to ordinary lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for writers 'with some sort of a dream' who 'see just a little bit more in the pedlar he passes on the street than you or I do' and show curiosity about 'the ragman's story' or the 'boot-black'—value diverse racial and cultural traditions contributing to a national literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value original perspectives, curiosity about marginalized or ordinary characters, and cultural diversity that enriches national literature not grounded in a single racial feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑readability / merit for a second reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of greater distinction 'may lay convincing claim to a second reading, because each of them has survived both tests, the test of substance and the test of form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a story rewards rereading (depth, layered meaning, craft) as evidence of higher quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest distinction: unity of substance, form, and sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: A small group possess 'the distinction of uniting genuine substance and artistic form in a closely woven pattern with such sincerity that these stories may fairly claim a position in our literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve special praise/publication for stories that tightly integrate organic substance and formal artistry with sincere purpose; these are candidates for republication/rolls of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asterisk/grouping scoring system
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are classified into four groups: (1) fail to survive either test (listed without comment), (2) survive either substance or form (indicated by a single asterisk), (3) survive both tests and may claim a second reading (two asterisks), (4) unite genuine substance and form with sincerity and are listed in 'Roll of Honor' (three asterisks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the asterisk system as shorthand for evaluative outcome: no mark = fail, * = passes one test, ** = passes both tests (worthy of second reading), *** = highest distinction/roll of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural selection rules for the annual volume
rubrics_metrics.description: "It has been a point of honor with me not to republish an English story, nor a translation from a foreign author. I have also made it a rule not to include more than one story by an individual author in the volume."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include English (non‑American) stories or translations; include at most one story per author in the anthology. Selection limited to stories published in American magazines during the defined period (October 1919 – September 1920).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetical arrangement is not ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: "The order in which the stories in this volume are printed is not intended as an indication of their comparative excellence; the arrangement is alphabetical by authors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present chosen stories alphabetically to avoid implying rank; clarify that placement does not equal qualitative ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor’s impartiality and allowance for modest personal preference
rubrics_metrics.description: "In compiling these lists, I have permitted no personal preference or prejudice to consciously influence my judgment. To the titles of certain stories, however, in the 'Rolls of Honor,' an asterisk is prefixed, and this asterisk, I must confess, reveals in some measure a personal preference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for impartial, objective selection by stated criteria, but allow that small, transparently marked personal preferences may be acknowledged.
